what: Toggle linkage. Motor A turns a crank whose pin drives a Scotch yoke along one axis: the yoke pin sits at 40·cos θ LDU (16·cos θ mm). A 1x3 link joins the yoke pin to the input hole of a 3L lever that pivots on a fixed vertical axle, 20 LDU (8 mm) from the pivot; the lever's far hole, 16 mm from the pivot, is its tip. The program turns the crank 0 → 85 → 0 degrees at 30 °/s. The yoke, link and lever are passive. In the simulator the lever follows the closed-loop link geometry within 0.02° up to θ = 60°, and reaches about 50° at θ = 85° against a predicted 49.0°. A crank and Scotch yoke push a short link against a lever pivoted at its end. As the crank nears 90°, the link folds back over the lever arm and its turning leverage collapses toward a dead centre, where the link pushes straight through the pivot. The passive lever follows the link-closure geometry within 0.02° up to 60°; the program stops at 85°, 5° short of dead centre.
try: Load the model, press Reset, then Run. The program refuses to start if motor A is more than 2° away from its saved zero.

Watch the lever while the crank turns at a steady 30 °/s. The yoke moves slowly at first and faster later, while the lever keeps turning at 3 to 4° per millimetre of yoke travel. Look at the link: it swings from square-on to the lever arm (90°) toward lying back along it.
Use the manual jog on port A in 5° steps from 60° to 85°. At each step, estimate the angle between the link and the lever's input arm. It falls from about 41° to about 7°.
Do not jog to 90°. There the link lies exactly over the pivot, and the geometry no longer decides which way the lever turns next. That is why the program and the jog both stop at 85°.
why: The yoke pin Y, the lever pivot P and the lever pin L form a triangle with |PL| = 20 LDU, |YL| = 40 LDU and a third side d = |PY| that changes as the yoke moves. For each d there are two mirror-image ways to close the triangle; the build starts on one of them, and the lever angle follows it continuously. When θ approaches 90°, the yoke pin comes level with the pivot and d shrinks toward 40 − 20 = 20 LDU, so the link folds back over the lever arm. The link can only push along its own line, so only the part of its force at right angles to the arm turns the lever: torque = F·r·sin μ, where μ is the angle between link and arm. μ falls from 90° at the start to 7° at 85°, so only sin 7° ≈ 12% of the link force still turns the lever, and at 90° none does: the link pushes straight through the pivot. This is a dead centre. Near it, a small amount of play or elasticity in a joint becomes a large lever error. That is why the simulated lever reads about 1° high at 85° but matches within 0.02° at 60°.
matters: Every crank and connecting-rod engine passes two dead centres per turn. Steam engines and single-cylinder engines carry them through on flywheel momentum, and locomotives set two cylinders 90° apart. Toggle clamps, stone crushers and toggle presses use the same alignment the other way round: driven from the lever side, the nearly straight link turns a small torque into a very large push, and it can lock just past the straight position. Designers watch the transmission angle μ and usually keep it above 40° or so, unless the dead centre is exactly the effect they want.
question: At a crank angle of 85°, the link makes an angle of about 7° with the lever arm. What fraction of the force along the link still turns the lever, and what happens at 90°?
answer: Only sin 7° ≈ 0.12, about 12% of the link force, still acts at right angles to the 8 mm arm and turns the lever. At 90° the link points straight through the pivot, so it produces no turning torque at all (a dead centre), and the geometry no longer decides which way the lever goes next.
further: Use the formula to predict the lever angle at θ = 30°, 60° and 75° (8.6°, 28.8° and 40.8°), then jog to those angles and compare.
Plot the lever angle against the yoke position instead of the crank angle. Why does the slope stay between about 3 and 4° per millimetre, even though the transmission angle collapses?
Sketch what would happen beyond 90° on each closing branch. Which real machines add a flywheel, a second phase-shifted crank or a mechanical stop to get through, or to stay at, this point?
formula: Y = (40·cos θ, 100) LDU, P = (0, 120) LDU; d = |PY|. Lever pin angle φ = atan2(Y−P) ± arccos((20² + d² − 40²)/(2·20·d)), on the branch continuous from φ(0) = 36.87°. Lever rotation = φ − 36.87°; transmission angle μ = the angle between the link YL and the arm PL; lever torque = F_link · 8 mm · sin μ.
